The rain in lower Oakhaven did not fall so much as hang, suspended in the amber halo of gaslamps like crushed glass. Arthur stood behind the mahogany counter of the Vault of Unspoken Things, polishing a brass loupe with the edge of his sleeve. Outside, the cobblestone alley gleamed like the carapace of a beetle, reflecting the neon sign from the apothecary across the street.

Arthur was seventy-two, or perhaps seventy-three. The tally of years had lost its sharpness, blurred by decades spent measuring the weight of human sentiment. On the shelves lining his shop sat hundreds of delicate glass spheres, each no larger than a plum, swirling with faint smoke. Some burned with a furious, crimson heat; those were old grudges, bitter and stubborn. Others glowed with a cool sapphire stillness, containing grief quieted by time.

The glass was blown from sand pulled from deep ocean trenches. It possessed a singular property: it could hold a concentrated moment of human experience without shattering, provided the memory was surrendered of the owner’s free will. People came to Arthur when the weight inside their minds grew too severe. He paid them in silver coins, took their burdens, and arranged them upon his shelves, waiting for collectors who traded in borrowed sensations.

A brass bell mounted above the oak door chimed, its sharp ring slicing through the shop’s quiet silence. A gust of night air swept inside, bringing the scents of wet wool and street mud.

Arthur looked up over his spectacles.

A young woman stood upon the threshold, shivering. Her winter coat was soaked at the shoulders, and her dark hair clung to her cheeks in damp spirals. She pressed her arm against her ribs, holding an unseen object beneath her cloak like a bird caught in a gale.

"We are closed for the evening, miss," Arthur said softly. His voice had the rustling cadence of dried leaves across stone.

"Please," she said, her voice thin. "The innkeeper said you were the only practitioner in the city who would not demand a name."

Arthur set his cloth down. He examined her face—the hollowed cheeks, the shadows beneath her eyes, the tremor in her lip. He knew that look. It was the quiet expression of a soul drowning while standing upright.

"I do not ask for names," Arthur said, stepping around the counter. "I only assess the trade. Come inside out of the draft."

She stepped into the warmth, her boots clicking against the timber floor. With hesitation, she pulled her hands from her cloak and laid her offering upon the velvet pad on the counter.

It was not yet bound in glass. It was raw emotion. A pulse of golden light rested in the palm of her glove, humming softly at a low frequency. It cast a rich radiance across the counter, driving away the chill.

Arthur leaned forward in quiet surprise. Pure golden light was an extraordinary rarity. Most patrons sought to purge regret, shame, or grief. Gold was the hue of untarnished happiness.

"You wish to part with a golden moment?" Arthur asked softly. "Most keep these locked in their hearts until death."

"It is far too bright," she whispered, her eyes fixed on the ember. "When I am in the dark, remembering it reminds me of what can never return. The sharpness of what I lost makes the present impossible to endure. It is not a comfort, sir. It is a brand burning into my flesh."

Arthur nodded in solemn understanding. The agony of remembered joy in times of ruin was an old poison.

"I understand," he said. He reached beneath the counter and produced a blank glass sphere and a silver siphon. "Once bound, the feeling will leave you completely. You will remember the facts of the day, but you will no longer feel its warmth. It will become a plain sentence in an old book. Are you certain?"

"Take it," she replied.

Arthur lifted the siphon. With practiced precision, he touched the tip to the golden light. The pulse quivered, then turned into luminous mist, flowing into the glass sphere. He sealed the opening with cobalt wax, pressing his brass seal into the crown.

As the wax cooled, Arthur touched the sphere to confirm the stability of the seal.

A rush of warmth flooded his mind.

A sunlit afternoon in late July. The smell of clover and dry earth. Laughing while running barefoot down a hillside, holding a hand that fit perfectly into her own. A quiet promise spoken beneath an old apple tree, light and unburdened by the future.

Arthur pulled his fingers away, breath catching in his throat. He blinked to clear his vision. It was exquisite—a crystal moment of pure belonging.

He looked at the young woman. Her shoulders had relaxed. The desperate strain in her features was gone, replaced by a blank stillness. Her eyes were quiet now, stripped of terror and light.
